newsitem.title: UK: Fund targets assets of cash-strapped Ukrainians.
newsitem.headline: Fund targets assets of cash-strapped Ukrainians.

text.p: Emerging market fund specialist Caspian aims to raise $150 million from western investors to purchase privatisation vouchers held by cash-strapped Ukrainian people for just one fortieth of their face value.

Caspian, which has linked up with local fund manager Kievskaya Rus Financial Investment, said on Thursday that investment vehicle, the Ukraine Privatisation Co, can buy vouchers which are worth $280 each for just $7.00 to $9.00.
"If you offer a rural Ukrainian cash for his vouchers, he will take it because there is so little money in the country," Christopher Derricott, a partner in Caspian told bankers in London.
The vouchers were being distributed to citizens and represent shares in companies which are being privatised.
The western fund is using Kievskaya Rus' network of 1,000 commission agents to access compensation certificates.
"It is like an enormous tupperware party," said Derricott.

The certificates were handed out to the population for the erosion of savings when inflation hit 10,000 percent in 1993 and trade at $1.60, compared with a face value of $5.70 and are accessible only to domestic investment funds.
"We have a huge discount between the real price and the face value of these certificates and vouchers because of the absence of money," said Vladimir Gerasymchuk, president of Kievskaya Rus.
Ukraine Privatisation Co will use the vouchers to buy stakes of seven to 10 percent in a list of 20 companies from the 208 which are being sold in Ukraine's current privatisation round.
Investors will be hoping for a quick return from their investments and an acceleration of trading on the somewhat sickly Kiev bourse.
So far, only five securities are trading and plans to start an over the counter market have come to nought.
"The 2,000-odd companies that have been sold are mostly lemons," said the Economist Intelligence Unit in its third quarter report on the country.

There are already some western investors. Goldman Sachs has a stake in the $8.0 million Ukrainian Growth Fund, which has bought shares from employees of privatised companies, sometimes by waiting at factory gates, according to the EIU.
As well as the pickup of the value of the investments from the discount at which they are trading, Caspian believes that a return to economic growth in Ukraine will deliver further benefits.
Caspian analyst Allan Roopan expects the economy to grow two percent next year after it collapsed in the wake of the breakup of the Soviet Union.
